overview: Guy of Lusignan was king of Jerusalem through marriage to Sibylla and the ruler whose defeat at Hattin preceded Saladin’s capture of Jerusalem.
His reputation is often negative because of Hattin, but his later Cypriot rule became a durable crusader-state legacy.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Guy of Lusignan was king of Jerusalem through marriage to Sibylla and the ruler whose defeat at Hattin preceded Saladin’s capture of Jerusalem.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Guy came from the Lusignan family of Poitou and entered the Latin East through aristocratic marriage and factional politics.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Guy of Lusignan is remembered, largely unkindly, as the king whose poor judgement led to the catastrophic loss of the kingdom at the Battle of Hattin in 1187. The sources present a handsome but politically lightweight noble who rose through marriage to Sibylla of Jerusalem, and whose indecision and susceptibility to bad counsel — especially that of the hawkish faction urging battle — are blamed for marching the army to destruction in the waterless hills before Hattin.

The hostile tradition, shaped by the magnitude of the disaster and by his aristocratic rivals, may exaggerate his incapacity; he was placed in an impossible position by a divided kingdom and aggressive enemies. Yet even sympathetic accounts struggle to credit him with the strength a ruler in crisis needed, and his later loss of the throne and consolation with the lordship of Cyprus did little to rehabilitate him.

What the record conveys is a man elevated by marriage beyond his political weight, remembered as well-meaning but weak and easily led. He is remembered chiefly as the king of Hattin — the ruler whose fatal decision lost Jerusalem — a figure of tragic inadequacy more than of malice, blamed by a tradition that needed someone to hold responsible for the great disaster.

contentSections.title: As king of Jerusalem and Cyprus
paragraphs: Guy’s authority was contested by nobles who doubted his judgment. At Hattin in 1187, his army was trapped and destroyed by Saladin, leading to the loss of Jerusalem. Later he became ruler of Cyprus.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Guy died in 1194 after establishing Lusignan rule on Cyprus, a kingdom that outlasted the mainland crusader kingdom.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: His reputation is often negative because of Hattin, but his later Cypriot rule became a durable crusader-state legacy.

succession.note: Guy reigned as Sibylla's consort; after losing Jerusalem he bought Cyprus from the Templars in 1192.
